rv.q: The mature audience members at my performance leaned in, all right, clearly well aware they were back at a great Chicago theater, listening to the words of one of the greatest playwrights ever born...

What’s perhaps most surprising here is that the casting dynamics end up placing greater-than-usual emphasis on the supporting characters, and in this production, under Les Waters’ direction, wildly excels.
A brilliant combination that makes Steppenwolf’s “No Man’s Land” an actor’s treat and an audience’s delight.
Steppenwolf has given it a definitive production, set in the soaring library of Hirst, a British aristocrat litterateur who has picked up Spooner, an aging poet, at a pub earlier.

This thoughtful, beautifully executed production conveys the full dark power of Pinter’s vision, subtly implicating the audience for finding pleasure and humor in the play’s starkly compelling depiction of a corrupt, decaying civilization.
This production, authoritatively directed by Les Waters, most rewards viewers who don't sweat the details and instead connect with the primal truths Pinter and these fine actors reveal...
Waters' sure-handed staging is characterized by a judicious use of Pinter pauses and a keen comedic sensibility.
Whatever you take from this play, one of Pinter's best and certainly funniest works, there is no denying that these men are stuck.

But Waters’s production and the can’t-take-your-eyes-off-them ensemble fill each pause and seeming non sequitur with a blend of pathos, humor, and clear-eyed understanding that the bravado of old men (and old nations) often hides aching voids.
Perry and Ulrich share the stage in a delicate balance that’s a treasure to behold.

And Pinter’s vision of the emotional and physical condition of his characters — men attempting to function in a “no man’s land,” who are torn between success and failure, plagued by problematic sexual desires and are increasingly aware of their mortality — remains intriguing as well as tragicomic.
The problem is that the play, while the script is often humorous or poetic, is confusing and difficult to derive meaning from.
Bravo to Waters for as fine a work of direction as this reviewer has ever seen.
This show, directed by Les Waters on a set designed by Andrew Boyce is quite "talky" and because they are English, they do have accents.

cn.t: Critics praise Steppenwolf's "Pinteresque perfection," celebrating the production's masterful performances—particularly Jeff Perry and Mark Ulrich—and its skillful navigation of Pinter's enigmatic, darkly funny wordplay about aging and loneliness.
